cells.tense: You are in the open with the pen already moving and the ground still yours.
cells.ask: Set one small piece of the work down today, plainly, where someone can see it.
cells.core: You're standing where nothing has been decided yet, and the pen is already moving. Most people freeze here or rush, and you're doing neither. You pick up what the clearing left and set one piece, then the next, and you know why each one goes where it goes. Hands on material, moving at the size the material allows — the mechanism is running the way it should.\n\nIt isn't certainty and it doesn't need to be. It's the slow making of something that wasn't there before, at a scale you can actually hold. The pace is what keeps the shape visible, so keep it where you can still see what you're making and let it stay unfinished as long as it needs to.
cells.sheetLine: You're building in the open and the pace is yours.
cells.verb: building something new out of cleared ground, hands first
cells.place: the open field before the first mark

cells.tense: You are already bracing at a finished thing that nobody has started building yet.
cells.ask: Find one person who has built something like this and ask what they cut.
cells.core: You can see the finished structure and you're already living in it — measuring it, defending it, impatient with anyone who can't see it yet. The ground is still empty and you're arguing about the roof. The future pulls you past the only part where something actually gets made.\n\nThe work runs slower than the vision. Bracing against that keeps your hands busy holding a shape that hasn't arrived, and the material sits there waiting. Go ask someone who has built close to this what they left out. Their answer won't be yours, and it will put you back in the room with the material.

cells.tense: You stood where something could have started and you are still at that door.
cells.ask: Put one thing you've already decided into the world today, in its plainest form, and let it stand.
cells.core: The ground is cleared and you didn't step onto it. The field is open and you're not in it. At its best this is a person laying one small thing down without needing it finished or defended — the first stone set simply because setting it is the work. What happens instead is a standing at the edge, watching the ground stay empty while the cleared space keeps its shape.\n\nA better plan doesn't move this and more energy doesn't either. One definite thing put where it can be seen — that's the act, and it costs nothing but being visible. It also restores the sense that what you set down stays set down, and that is what makes the next act available.
cells.sheetLine: The field is open and you haven't stepped in.
cells.verb: building something new out of cleared ground, hands first
cells.place: the open field before the first mark

cells.tense: You are shaping what gets built here while calling yourself a spectator to it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you shaped this week that you've been describing as how it went.
cells.core: You're already in it — picking what gets carried, adjusting the plan, saying the thing that moves people. The building is going up around you and you talk like you arrived after it started. The hands are yours. The accounting isn't, and that gap is the whole thing.\n\nNone of this needs announcing or a title. It needs one moment where you catch yourself calling a choice how it went and admit you made it. Owning the moves already inside the structure is what makes the next choice yours — not more effort on the building, but claiming the pen sitting in your hand. Start with the smallest move you can find.
